title: UNIT 2: ELECTROCHEMISTRY
notes:
✓ Electrochemistry → The branch of chemistry that deals with the relationship between chemical reactions and electrical energy.
It mainly involves oxidation–reduction reactions, electrolysis, electrolytic cells, Faraday's laws, industrial electrochemical processes, and voltaic cells.

title: 2.1 Oxidation–Reduction Reactions
notes:
✓ Oxidation–reduction reactions, commonly called redox reactions → Chemical reactions involving the transfer of electrons from one species to another.
Oxidation and reduction always occur simultaneously because electrons lost by one substance must be gained by another.

◆ EXAMPLE
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

✓ Zinc loses electrons and is oxidized:
Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻

✓ Copper(II) ions gain electrons and are reduced:
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

→ Zinc is the reducing agent and Cu²⁺ is the oxidizing agent.

✓ Redox reactions are important in combustion, corrosion, respiration, metal extraction, batteries, electrolysis, and many industrial processes.

title: 2.1.1 Oxidation
notes:
✓ Oxidation → The process in which a substance loses one or more electrons.
✓ Oxidation is also indicated by an increase in oxidation number.

◆ OXIDATION CAN ALSO BE DESCRIBED AS
✓ Loss of electrons.
✓ Increase in oxidation number.
✓ Addition of oxygen.
✓ Removal of hydrogen.

◆ EXAMPLE
Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻

✓ Fe²⁺ loses one electron and its oxidation number increases from +2 to +3. Therefore, Fe²⁺ is oxidized.

◆ ANOTHER EXAMPLE
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

✓ Magnesium changes from oxidation number 0 to +2, so magnesium undergoes oxidation.

◆ MEMORY TIP
OIL → Oxidation Is Loss of electrons.

title: 2.1.2 Reduction
notes:
✓ Reduction → The process in which a substance gains one or more electrons.
✓ Reduction is also indicated by a decrease in oxidation number.

◆ REDUCTION CAN ALSO BE DESCRIBED AS
✓ Gain of electrons.
✓ Decrease in oxidation number.
✓ Removal of oxygen.
✓ Addition of hydrogen.

◆ EXAMPLE
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

✓ Copper(II) ions gain two electrons and their oxidation number decreases from +2 to 0. Therefore, Cu²⁺ is reduced.

◆ ANOTHER EXAMPLE
Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺

✓ The oxidation number decreases from +3 to +2, showing reduction.

◆ MEMORY TIP
RIG → Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

title: Oxidizing and Reducing Agents
notes:
✓ Oxidizing agent → A substance that causes another substance to be oxidized. It accepts electrons and is itself reduced.
✓ Reducing agent → A substance that causes another substance to be reduced. It donates electrons and is itself oxidized.

◆ EXAMPLE
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

✓ Zn loses electrons → Zn is the reducing agent.
✓ Cu²⁺ gains electrons → Cu²⁺ is the oxidizing agent.

◆ GENERAL RULE
Oxidizing agent → accepts electrons → is reduced.
Reducing agent → donates electrons → is oxidized.

✓ The substance that is oxidized is the reducing agent, while the substance that is reduced is the oxidizing agent.

title: Oxidation Number
notes:
✓ Oxidation number → The apparent charge assigned to an atom in a compound or ion according to specific rules.
✓ Oxidation numbers are useful for identifying which elements are oxidized or reduced and for balancing redox reactions.

◆ IMPORTANT RULES
✓ An element in its free state has oxidation number 0.
✓ A monatomic ion has an oxidation number equal to its charge.
✓ Oxygen is usually −2.
✓ Hydrogen is usually +1 when bonded to nonmetals.
✓ The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is 0.
✓ The sum of oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion equals the charge of the ion.

◆ EXAMPLE
Find the oxidation number of sulfur in H₂SO₄.

2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0
2 + S − 8 = 0
S = +6

✓ Sulfur has an oxidation number of +6.

→ Increase in oxidation number means oxidation.
→ Decrease in oxidation number means reduction.

title: 2.1.3 Balancing Oxidation–Reduction (Redox) Reactions
notes:
✓ A redox equation must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element and the total electrical charge are conserved.
✓ The two important methods are the oxidation-number method and the half-reaction method.

◆ OXIDATION-NUMBER METHOD
◆ 1. Write the unbalanced equation.
◆ 2. Assign oxidation numbers to the elements involved.
◆ 3. Identify the element oxidized and the element reduced.
◆ 4. Determine the increase and decrease in oxidation numbers.
◆ 5. Choose coefficients so that the total increase equals the total decrease.
◆ 6. Balance the remaining atoms.
◆ 7. Check both atoms and charge.

◆ HALF-REACTION METHOD
✓ Separate the reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions.

◆ EXAMPLE
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

Oxidation:
Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻

Reduction:
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

✓ Adding the two half-reactions gives:
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

✓ For reactions in acidic or basic aqueous solutions, H₂O, H⁺, OH⁻, and electrons may be used to balance atoms and charge.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ The total number of electrons lost must equal the total number of electrons gained.

title: 2.2 Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions
notes:
✓ Electrolysis → The process in which electrical energy is used to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
✓ In aqueous electrolysis, an electrolyte is dissolved in water and contains mobile ions that carry electric current.

✓ Positive ions, called cations, move toward the cathode.
✓ Negative ions, called anions, move toward the anode.

→ Cathode → Reduction
→ Anode → Oxidation

✓ Water can also participate in electrolysis, so the ions originally present in the solute are not always the species discharged at the electrodes.

title: 2.2.1 Electrolytic Cells
notes:
✓ Electrolytic cell → An electrochemical cell in which an external source of electrical energy forces a non-spontaneous redox reaction to occur.

◆ MAIN PARTS
✓ Electrolyte.
✓ Two electrodes.
✓ External direct-current power source.

✓ The cathode is connected to the negative terminal of the power source. Positive ions move toward the cathode and are reduced.
✓ The anode is connected to the positive terminal. Negative ions or other species are oxidized at the anode.

◆ ELECTRODE SIGNS
Cathode → negative
Anode → positive

◆ ELECTRODE REACTIONS
Anode → oxidation
Cathode → reduction

◆ MEMORY TIP
AN OX → Anode Oxidation.
RED CAT → Reduction Cathode.

title: 2.2.2 Preferential Discharge
notes:
✓ Preferential discharge → The process in which one ion is discharged at an electrode more readily than another competing ion.

✓ When an aqueous solution contains several ions, more than one species may be capable of being oxidized or reduced.

◆ FACTORS AFFECTING PREFERENTIAL DISCHARGE
✓ Relative ease of oxidation or reduction.
✓ Concentration of the ions.
✓ Nature of the electrode.
✓ Presence of water and competing reactions.
✓ Overpotential or overvoltage effects.

✓ At the cathode, cations compete for reduction.
✓ At the anode, anions and water may compete for oxidation.

◆ EXAMPLE: AQUEOUS NaCl
✓ Na⁺ competes with water at the cathode. Under ordinary conditions, water is preferentially reduced:
2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻

✓ At the anode, chloride ions can be oxidized:
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ In aqueous electrolysis, always consider water as a possible competitor at both electrodes.

title: 2.2.3 Electrolysis of Selected Aqueous Solutions
notes:
✓ Different aqueous electrolytes produce different substances at the electrodes depending on the ions present and their preferential discharge.

◆ AQUEOUS SODIUM CHLORIDE (NaCl)
Cathode:
2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻

Anode:
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

Overall reaction:
2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂

✓ Hydrogen is produced at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and sodium hydroxide remains in the solution.

◆ AQUEOUS COPPER(II) SULFATE (CuSO₄) WITH INERT ELECTRODES
Cathode:
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

✓ Copper metal is deposited at the cathode.

Anode:
2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻

✓ Oxygen is produced at the anode.

◆ AQUEOUS CuSO₄ WITH COPPER ELECTRODES
Anode:
Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻

Cathode:
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

✓ Copper is transferred from the anode to the cathode. This principle is used in copper electrorefining.

title: 2.3 Quantitative Aspects of Electrolysis
notes:
✓ The amount of material deposited or liberated during electrolysis depends on the quantity of electrical charge passing through the electrolyte.

◆ ELECTRIC CHARGE
Q = It

✓ Q → Electric charge in coulombs (C)
✓ I → Current in amperes (A)
✓ t → Time in seconds (s)

◆ FARADAY CONSTANT
F = 9.65 × 10⁴ C mol⁻¹

✓ The charge carried by one mole of electrons is approximately one Faraday.

◆ MOLES OF ELECTRONS
moles of electrons = Q/F
moles of electrons = It/F

◆ FOR AN ION Mⁿ⁺
Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M

✓ n moles of electrons are required to produce one mole of M.

✓ This relationship allows the mass of a substance deposited or liberated during electrolysis to be calculated.

title: 2.3.1 Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis
notes:
✓ Faraday's First Law → The mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

m ∝ Q

Since:
Q = It

then:
m ∝ It

◆ ELECTROCHEMICAL EQUIVALENT
m = ZQ
m = ZIt

✓ Z → Electrochemical equivalent.
✓ The electrochemical equivalent is the mass of a substance deposited or liberated by one coulomb of electricity.

◆ RELATIONSHIP WITH MOLAR MASS
Z = M/nF

Therefore:
m = MIt/nF

✓ Increasing the current or increasing the time of electrolysis increases the amount of substance deposited, provided other conditions remain constant.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Convert time to seconds before using Q = It.

title: 2.3.2 Faraday's Second Law of Electrolysis
notes:
✓ Faraday's Second Law → When the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes, the masses of substances deposited or liberated are proportional to their equivalent masses.

m₁/m₂ = E₁/E₂

◆ EQUIVALENT MASS
E = M/n

✓ M → Molar mass.
✓ n → Number of electrons involved in the electrode reaction.

Therefore:
m₁/m₂ = (M₁/n₁)/(M₂/n₂)

◆ EXAMPLE
Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

✓ The equivalent masses of silver and copper are different because different numbers of electrons are involved in their reduction reactions.

◆ REMEMBER
✓ For the same quantity of electricity, the mass deposited depends on the equivalent mass of the substance.

title: 2.4 Industrial Applications of Electrolysis
notes:
✓ Electrolysis has many important industrial applications. It is used for extracting reactive metals, purifying metals, producing important chemicals, and coating objects with metals.

◆ METAL EXTRACTION
✓ Highly reactive metals such as aluminium cannot be easily extracted by ordinary chemical reduction with carbon. Electrolysis is used to obtain them from their compounds.

At the cathode:
Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al

◆ ELECTROREFINING
✓ Electrolysis is used to purify metals such as copper.
✓ In copper refining, impure copper is used as the anode and pure copper is used as the cathode.

Anode:
Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻

Cathode:
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

✓ Pure copper is deposited on the cathode while some impurities collect as anode sludge.

◆ ELECTROPLATING
✓ Electroplating → The process of depositing a thin layer of one metal onto another material using electrolysis.
✓ The object being coated is generally connected to the cathode, where metal ions are reduced and deposited.

Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M

✓ Electroplating improves appearance, corrosion resistance, durability, and surface properties.

◆ INDUSTRIAL CHEMICAL PRODUCTION
✓ Electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride produces sodium hydroxide, chlorine, and hydrogen:
2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂

✓ These products are widely used in chemical manufacturing and other industries.

title: 2.5 Voltaic Cells
notes:
✓ Voltaic cell, also called a galvanic cell → An electrochemical cell that converts chemical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.

✓ Unlike an electrolytic cell, a voltaic cell does not require an external electrical source to force the reaction. Instead, the spontaneous reaction produces an electrical potential that can drive electrons through an external circuit.

◆ SIMPLE Zn–Cu VOLTAIC CELL
✓ One half-cell contains zinc metal in a solution containing Zn²⁺ ions.
✓ The other contains copper metal in a solution containing Cu²⁺ ions.
✓ The half-cells are connected by an external conducting wire and a salt bridge.

At the zinc electrode, oxidation occurs:
Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻

✓ Zinc is the anode.

At the copper electrode, reduction occurs:
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

✓ Copper is the cathode.

◆ OVERALL REACTION
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

→ Electrons flow through the external circuit from the zinc anode toward the copper cathode.

title: Salt Bridge in a Voltaic Cell
notes:
✓ Salt bridge → A connection between the two half-cells of a voltaic cell that allows ions to migrate between them.

◆ FUNCTIONS
✓ Maintains electrical neutrality in the half-cells.
✓ Completes the internal electrical circuit.
✓ Allows continued movement of ions.
✓ Prevents the rapid direct mixing of the two electrolytes.

✓ As zinc is oxidized, Zn²⁺ ions accumulate in the zinc half-cell. Anions from the salt bridge migrate toward this compartment to help maintain electrical neutrality.

✓ At the copper half-cell, Cu²⁺ ions are consumed during reduction. Cations from the salt bridge migrate toward this compartment to compensate for the change in charge.

✓ Without a suitable ion pathway, charge would accumulate and the redox reaction would eventually stop.

title: Electrode Signs in Voltaic Cells
notes:
✓ In a voltaic cell, the anode is the negative electrode and the cathode is the positive electrode.

Anode = negative → oxidation
Cathode = positive → reduction

✓ The zinc electrode in a Zn–Cu cell is negative because oxidation at the zinc electrode releases electrons. These electrons then travel through the external circuit toward the copper cathode.

✓ The names anode and cathode are determined by the reaction occurring at the electrodes, not by their signs.

◆ MOST IMPORTANT RULES
Anode → oxidation.
Cathode → reduction.

✓ These rules apply to both voltaic and electrolytic cells.

title: Voltaic Cell vs Electrolytic Cell
notes:
◆ VOLTAIC CELL
✓ Converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
✓ Uses a spontaneous redox reaction.
✓ Produces electrical energy.
✓ Anode is negative.
✓ Cathode is positive.
✓ Oxidation occurs at the anode.
✓ Reduction occurs at the cathode.

◆ ELECTROLYTIC CELL
✓ Converts electrical energy into chemical energy.
✓ Uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.
✓ Consumes electrical energy.
✓ Anode is positive.
✓ Cathode is negative.
✓ Oxidation occurs at the anode.
✓ Reduction occurs at the cathode.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ The electrode signs are different, but the reaction locations never change:
Anode → oxidation.
Cathode → reduction.

title: ELECTROCHEMISTRY — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
OIL → Oxidation Is Loss of electrons.
RIG → Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

Oxidation → oxidation number increases.
Reduction → oxidation number decreases.

Oxidizing agent → accepts electrons → is reduced.
Reducing agent → donates electrons → is oxidized.

Anode → oxidation.
Cathode → reduction.

◆ ELECTROLYTIC CELL
Electrical energy → chemical energy.

◆ VOLTAIC CELL
Chemical energy → electrical energy.

◆ IMPORTANT FORMULAS
Q = It
F = 9.65 × 10⁴ C mol⁻¹
m = ZQ
m = ZIt
Z = M/nF
m = MIt/nF
E = M/n
m₁/m₂ = E₁/E₂
